item.title: Microsoft launches Maia 300, third‑generation in‑house AI inference chip
item.description:
Microsoft launches Maia 300, third‑generation in‑house AI inference chip

Microsoft announced its third‑generation Maia 300 AI chip today, positioning it as the primary AI inference system for the company’s products and services.

🔍 Overview

  • Maia 300 is designed to improve the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud.
  • It is built to handle the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks.
  • The chip reduces Microsoft’s reliance on Nvidia GPUs and AMD solutions.
  • Production roll‑out is planned for 2027, with multi‑gigawatt Azure deployments beginning the same year.

🧩 How it works

  • Microsoft uses a chiplet architecture to gain efficiency gains.
  • The chip is fabricated on TSMC’s N2P process node.
  • Maia 300 separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions into distinct chiplets, which “increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” said the Azure hardware and infrastructure team.

⚙️ Key details

  • Performance: “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU‑based systems,” said Scott Guthrie, EVP of Microsoft’s cloud group.
  • Scale: In a full 96‑accelerator configuration, Maia 300 delivers up to 7× the rack‑scale token throughput of Maia 200.
  • Workload focus: “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long‑context reasoning, latency‑sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi‑step agentic tasks,” according to Microsoft.
  • Successor: Maia 300 follows Maia 200, which was announced in January and is already running production workloads such as Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models.
Chip Current Use Notable Claim
Maia 200 Production workloads (Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, internal models) “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real‑world metrics for AI services,” – Scott Guthrie
Maia 300 Planned production rollout in 2027; primary inference system for Microsoft services “40 percent more tokens per megawatt” and “up to 7× rack‑scale token throughput” compared with Maia 200

🚀 Availability

  • Maia 300 will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027.
  • Microsoft plans to scale the Azure Maia family to multi‑gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making the chip the primary inference platform for its services.

💡 Why it matters

  • The efficiency improvements allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its own AI chips rather than third‑party GPUs.
  • Owning the silicon stack enables tighter co‑design with Microsoft’s AI models, a priority expressed by AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman: “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon… running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”
  • The chip is intended to help Microsoft catch up with leading AI research organizations such as Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic.

#Microsoft #AIChip #Maia300 #Azure #Inference

Source: Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs

item.title: Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers
item.description:
Multi-Node LLM Inference on Amazon EKS with Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers

This post shows how to deploy one large language model (LLM) across two GPU nodes on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the multi‑node Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers. The deployment separates the prefill and decode phases onto distinct GPU workers behind a single OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.

🔍 Overview

  • Ray is a distributed compute framework; Ray Serve deployments can span multiple nodes.
  • AWS Deep Learning Containers (DLCs) are pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images that bundle a framework, its dependencies, and the GPU stack into a tested, patched combination you can pull and use immediately.
  • The new Ray LLM DLC extends this approach to multi‑node inference.

🏗️ Architecture

  • CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) runs system workloads, the KubeRay operator, and the Ray head pod (CPU‑only).
  • Two GPU worker nodes (g6.8xlarge) run Ray workers: one dedicated to the prefill phase, the other to the decode phase.
  • Both GPU nodes pull the Ray LLM DLC from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR).
  • KubeRay watches the RayService you apply and automatically wires the head‑to‑worker join.
  • Ray Serve places the prefill and decode deployments on the two GPU workers.
  • KV‑cache generated by prefill is transferred to the decode worker over NIXL, using the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) through NIXL’s libfabric backend.

⚙️ How It Works

  • Prefill phase
    • Processes the entire input prompt in parallel.
    • Builds the key‑value (KV) cache.
    • Compute‑bound.
  • Decode phase
    • Generates the response one token at a time, reading and extending the KV cache.
    • Memory‑bandwidth‑bound.
  • Separating the phases prevents compute‑heavy long prompts from stalling token generation for requests already in progress.
  • Disaggregation allows each phase to use hardware and serving properties tuned to its workload, improving overall performance at scale.
  • The trade‑off is that the KV cache must be handed from prefill to decode quickly enough to retain the benefit.

📦 Key Components

Component Role
Ray LLM DLC Packages Ray Serve LLM, NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL), and the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) stack; exposes an OpenAI‑compatible API with no application code
vLLM Inference engine
Ray Serve HTTP Serving layer
NIXL KV‑cache transfer between nodes
EFA stack (libfabric, aws‑ofi‑nccl) High‑bandwidth node‑to‑node communication
AWS Deep Learning Containers Pre‑built, performance‑optimized Docker images ensuring no version drift between CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer

🚀 Deployment Details

  • The Ray LLM DLC ships Ray Serve LLM, NIXL, and the EFA stack, ready for multi‑node inference.
  • No application code is required to expose the OpenAI‑compatible endpoint.
  • This multi‑node setup is common for tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism, as well as for prefill/decode disaggregation inference workloads.
  • In a previous post, the Ray Serve DLC was used to stand up a small model behind an HTTP endpoint on a single GPU node.

💡 Why It Matters

  • By assigning prefill and decode to separate GPUs, compute‑heavy prefill work no longer contends with latency‑sensitive decode work.
  • Independent scaling of each phase enables better resource utilization and lower latency for LLM serving at scale.
  • All components are validated together before each release, guaranteeing compatibility across the CUDA runtime, framework, and serving layer.

#AWS #Ray #LLM #Kubernetes #Inference

Source: Run multi-node inference workloads using Ray LLM Deep Learning Containers | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Updates Inference Capabilities and OpenAI Compatibility
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI Updates Inference Capabilities and OpenAI Compatibility

Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced new capabilities for deploying and consuming AI models, offering users paths for managed infrastructure or Kubernetes-native control with Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference. In 2026, the platform delivered 13 new features to improve model deployment and optimization.

🔍 Overview

SageMaker AI now supports two primary deployment paths:

  • Managed endpoints: AWS handles infrastructure, operations, GPU provisioning, scaling, and monitoring.
  • Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference: Provides Kubernetes-native control for dedicated GPU clusters.

🧩 How it works

Inference recommendations automate the process of optimizing models based on performance goals such as cost, latency, or throughput. The system performs a three-step process:

  • Narrow: Filters instance types by analyzing model architecture and requirements.
  • Optimize: Applies techniques such as EAGLE 3.0 speculative decoding, kernel tuning, and tensor parallelism.
  • Benchmark: Runs NVIDIA AIPerf on real GPU infrastructure with multi-run confidence reporting.

⚙️ Key details

SageMaker now exposes an /openai/v1 path supporting Chat Completions with streaming, allowing for migration by simply updating the endpoint URL. Other technical improvements include:

  • Heterogeneous fleets: Customers can prioritize up to five instance types, with SageMaker automatically handling fallback and scaling based on capacity.
  • Optimized configurations: Each pool entry can reference unique configurations like quantization or speculative decoding generated by inference recommendations.
  • Metrics: Output includes validated metrics such as time to first token (TTFT), inter-token latency (ITL), and throughput.

🚀 Availability

These features are supported for single-model, inference component, and async endpoints in all commercial AWS Regions. There is no additional cost for generating recommendations, and customers with ML Reservations can benchmark on reserved capacity at no extra charge.

💡 Comparison of Inference Paths

Feature Managed SageMaker Inference SageMaker HyperPod Inference
Infrastructure Fully managed by AWS Managed Kubernetes stack
Deploy target Console, SDK, CLI kubectl, Terraform, Console, CLI, SDK
Scaling Managed auto scaling Auto scaling with Karpenter, KEDA, CloudWatch
API protocol OpenAI compatible HTTP, gRPC and custom load balancer

#AWS #SageMaker #MachineLearning #CloudComputing #Inference

Source: Amazon SageMaker Inference: 2026 year-to-date launches in review | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Amazon SageMaker Inference Introduces Prefix-Aware Routing
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker Inference Introduces Prefix-Aware Routing

Amazon SageMaker Inference has introduced prefix-aware routing, a new routing strategy designed to optimize how requests are handled by instances.

🧩 How it works

Prefix-aware routing analyzes the beginning of each request payload to determine which instance should handle it. Its primary functions include:

  • Consistency: Requests with the same beginning are consistently sent to the same instance.
  • Distribution: Different beginnings are spread across different instances.
  • Cache Optimization: If multiple requests share a prefix, they are routed to the same machine to keep that machine’s cache warm.
  • Automated Management: The endpoint handles routing based on request content; users do not need to manage affinity or tag requests.
  • Load Balancing: If a target instance is at capacity due to a popular prefix, the endpoint routes the request to a less busy instance.
  • Stability: Most requests continue going to the same instance when instances are added or removed.

⚙️ Key details

Amazon SageMaker Inference now offers three routing strategies for real-time endpoints:

Strategy Description
RANDOM The default routing strategy.
LEAST_OUTSTANDING_REQUESTS Routes based on outstanding requests.
PREFIX_AWARE New strategy that routes based on the request beginning.

Users can set the strategy per production variant in the endpoint configuration and switch between strategies without redeploying the model.

💡 Why it matters

In benchmarks using Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on 7 ml.p5.48xlarge instances with vLLM (prefix caching enabled), prefix-aware routing showed the following results compared to the random routing baseline:

General Impact

  • P50 TTFT reduced by up to 77 percent.
  • Throughput increased by up to 16 percent.
  • KV cache hit rates increased from roughly 25 percent to over 80 percent.

Specific Test Scenarios

  • 8,000-token shared prefixes (sustained over 1 hour):
    • P50 TTFT: Reduced by 71–77 percent.
    • P90 TTFT: Reduced by 33–37 percent.
    • Throughput: Increased 15–16 percent.
    • KV cache hit rate: Increased from approximately 25 to 82 percent.
  • Variable-length ShareGPT-style conversations (30 minutes):
    • P50 TTFT: Reduced by 13–16 percent.
    • P90 TTFT: Reduced by 24–37 percent.
    • Throughput: Increased 1.7–2.0 percent.
    • KV cache hit rate: Increased from approximately 30 to 80 percent.

Performance Overhead

  • The routing logic adds 1.3–1.9 milliseconds per request, while model TTFT in tests ranged from 63–280 milliseconds.
  • Traffic distribution remained balanced, with each of the 7 instances receiving 13.3–15.4 percent of requests.

#AmazonSageMaker #LLM #Inference #MachineLearning

Source: Reduce LLM latency with prefix-aware routing on Amazon SageMaker Inference | Amazon Web Services

item.title: NVIDIA NIM Optimizes Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B Performance on Blackwell GPUs
item.description:
NVIDIA NIM Optimizes Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B Performance on Blackwell GPUs

NVIDIA NIM provides model- and GPU-aware serving choices packaged into a deployable microservice, offering validated performance engineering alongside an enterprise-ready container lifecycle.

🔍 Overview

NIM allows for the deployment of models like nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b. For production environments, NIM Certified provides commercial support through NVIDIA AI Enterprise, CVE handling, regular inference-stack updates, and broader hardware validation.

🧩 How it works

The optimized NIM stack employs several technical strategies to improve efficiency:

  • Hardware Mapping: Autotuned Mamba and mixture-of-experts kernels map hybrid architectures to NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs.
  • Parallelism: Tensor parallelism distributes the model across four GPUs, while expert-aware execution improves utilization for mixture-of-experts layers.
  • Memory and Cache: Prefix caching prevents the recomputation of repeated context, while partial-prefix matching recovers reuse when only part of a prefix matches. Mamba state-cache settings are tuned for the model architecture.
  • Workload Management: The system uses batched-token limits, concurrent-sequence limits, GPU-memory allocation, and block size to maintain work in flight without exceeding latency targets.
  • Decoding: The stack utilizes MTP speculative decoding and associated fixes.

⚙️ Key details

Performance benchmarks for agentic workloads (64K/400/76% KV reuse/50 TPS/user with 20 ms ITL) on 4xB200 hardware are as follows:

Configuration Throughput Notes
NIM Off baseline 718 tok/s No NIM optimizations
NIM On (2.0.12) 1,997 tok/s 2.5x v. Baseline

🚀 Availability

Users can deploy this via the Nemotron 3 Ultra NIM page by accepting governing terms and selecting the NIM 2.0.12 tag or published digest. Implementation details include:

  • Tag: export NIM_TAG=2.0.12
  • Image: nvcr.io/nim/nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:$NIM_TAG
  • Optimized Profile: For agentic workloads on a four-GPU B200 system, use vllm-nvidia-b200-nvfp4-tp4-pp1-throughput-90.0 and enable speculative decoding.
  • Benchmarking: NVIDIA AIPerf can be used to replay representative traffic, utilizing Mooncake-format JSONL traces or captured NIM requests.

#NVIDIA #NIM #Blackwell #LLM #Inference

Source: How Full-Stack NIM Optimizations Deliver 2.5x More Users on Nemotron 3 Ultra | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Supports Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation for Multimodal Model Inference
item.description:
NVIDIA Dynamo Supports Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation for Multimodal Model Inference

NVIDIA Dynamo, an open source inference framework for distributed environments, now supports Encode-Prefill-Decode (EPD) disaggregation. This optimization technique improves multimodal model performance by separating the vision encoder stage from the prefill and decode stages.

🧩 How it works

Dynamo implements EPD serving by separating encoder and PD (prefill-decode) worker roles. Instead of running these phases with tightly coupled scheduling, they are treated as independently scalable stages:

  • Encoder Workers: Produce vision embeddings.
  • PD Workers: Consume those embeddings and run the LLM.
  • Data Transfer: The NVIDIA Inference Transfer Library (NIXL) is used to pass embeddings from encoder workers to PD workers.

⚙️ Key details

There are three primary placement options for these workers:

Placement Option Description
Aggregated Each GPU runs a single worker managing encoding, prefill, and decode for the entire request lifecycle.
Colocated Encoder Each GPU runs one or more encoder workers alongside one PD worker; generally the better fit for homogeneous clusters.
Disaggregated Encoder Encoder workers are placed on a lower-cost GPU tier while the primary GPU tier hosts PD workers.

In a test environment, two NVIDIA RTX 6000D GPUs were used for encoder workers, while four NVIDIA GB200 GPUs handled the PD workers. This configuration reserves the GB200 GPUs for the more memory- and compute-intensive LLM workload.

💡 Why it matters

EPD disaggregation isolates encoder work, which allows text requests to skip waiting for the encoder. This leads to improvements in batching, memory efficiency, and overall throughput.

Performance gains include:

  • Up to 5x faster time to first token (TTFT).
  • Up to 7x faster end-to-end response time.

The technique is most effective under the following conditions:

  • Image-heavy prompts.
  • Short-to-medium outputs.
  • Quantized mixture-of-experts (MoE) and lower-precision models (e.g., Qwen3.5 122B A10B NVFP4).
  • Scenarios where vision encoding accounts for a significant share of processing time or limits throughput.

Large dense models see less gain from this optimization.

#NVIDIA #Dynamo #LLM #MultimodalAI #Inference

Source: When to Use Encode-Prefill-Decode Disaggregation to Accelerate Multimodal Model Serving | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency
item.description:
Recent Developments in LLM KV Cache Compression and Efficiency

New research introduces two distinct approaches to optimizing key-value (KV) cache memory usage in large language models to address bottlenecks in long-context inference and reasoning workloads.

🔍 Overview

KV cache growth poses a significant memory bottleneck for LLM serving. Two new frameworks, GrowPage and SGD-KV, provide methods to manage cache memory more efficiently.

🧩 How it works

Framework Methodology Primary Focus
GrowPage On-demand budgeting Dynamically adjusts KV capacity based on runtime demand variations.
SGD-KV Summarization-Guided Compression Uses a head-aware diagnostic task to prioritize attention heads.

⚙️ Key details

GrowPage

  • Treats KV capacity as a runtime resource that evolves during generation.
  • Maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to estimate demand.
  • Integrates with PagedAttention to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
  • Adjusts capacity by compressing states or acquiring additional physical pages as needed.

SGD-KV

  • Employs a chunk-summarization diagnostic task to identify heads specialized in hierarchical information aggregation.
  • Reduces KV cache memory usage by up to 75%.
  • Maintains performance on benchmarks up to 1M context tokens.
  • Tested on Qwen2.5-7B-1M and Qwen3-32B models.

💡 Why it matters

Both methods offer improved performance-to-throughput or efficiency-to-accuracy trade-offs, enabling more effective long-context inference and reasoning.

#LLM #KVCache #AI #MachineLearning #Inference

Source: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving Source: SGD-KV: Summarization Guided KV Cache Compression

item.title: Nvidia Introduces Integrated Rubin‑Vera System for End‑to‑End Agent Workloads
item.description:
Nvidia Introduces Integrated Rubin‑Vera System for End‑to‑End Agent Workloads

Nvidia is expanding its focus from raw GPU horsepower to full‑stack hardware that can run agentic workloads from start to finish. By pairing Rubin GPUs with a Vera CPU and additional supporting units, the company aims to cut data movement and speed up the orchestration needed for multi‑step AI agents.

🛠️ Hardware Architecture

  • Rubin GPUs + Vera CPU – The combination is designed to keep data close to compute, reducing latency caused by moving information between separate components.
  • Supporting units – Additional hardware is included to further accelerate orchestration of complex, multi‑step agents.

⚡ Performance Highlights

  • Vera’s orchestration role is reported to deliver up to 3× improvements on certain I/O‑heavy operations.
  • The design shifts emphasis from GPU throughput alone to overall latency, memory orchestration, and data plumbing.

📦 Deployment Implications

  • Integrated racks that bundle CPU, GPU, flash storage, and accelerators are expected from hardware partners and cloud vendors.
  • This changes procurement and cost‑modeling decisions, as well as considerations about where sensitive workflows are deployed.

📈 Guidance for Founders and Operators

  • Stop treating the GPU as the whole stack; evaluate full‑stack latency and token cost (model inference plus orchestration overhead) against end‑to‑end hardware profiles.
  • When negotiating with cloud providers, request agent‑focused SLAs and detailed specifications of memory and access patterns before committing to large‑scale deployments.

✅ Key Takeaways

  • Agent performance now hinges on the entire hardware stack, not just GPU speed.
  • Nvidia’s Rubin‑Vera pairing promises notable I/O gains, potentially lowering the cost of running production agents.
  • Organizations should benchmark complete end‑to‑end latency and seek contracts that reflect the broader resource needs of agentic workloads.

#Nvidia #AIagents #Hardware #Inference #Deployment

Source: AI Agents News — Week of August 30, 2026 (Daily Updates)
